title: We Found +49R in Discovery — So We Stopped Optimizing the Strategy
author: BlackGreep
selftext:
We just finished the controlled Discovery refinement of our 1-minute scalping strategy.

The previous analysis showed something unusual:

LONG trades were negative on BTC, ETH and SOL.

SHORT trades were positive on all three.

Instead of testing dozens of new filters, we made exactly one predeclared change:

**Disable LONG. Keep everything else identical.**

No RSI tuning.

No RVOL tuning.

No TP changes.

No stop changes.

No regime filter.

No symbol-specific parameters.

Then we reran the full 90-day Discovery period causally.

Results:

**BTC**

\* 66 trades

\* Mean R: +0.096

\* Gross: +6.33R

**ETH**

\* 139 trades

\* Mean R: +0.164

\* Gross: +22.84R

**SOL**

\* 131 trades

\* Mean R: +0.152

\* Gross: +19.90R

**Combined**

\* 336 trades

\* Mean R: +0.146

\* Gross: +49.07R

All three markets stayed positive.

No single market accounted for more than 70% of the positive gross result.

That sounds encouraging.

But the temporal breakdown is much less comfortable:

**Month 1:** \+10.15R

**Month 2:** \+40.69R

**Month 3:** \-1.76R

SOL was particularly unstable across the three blocks.

And these numbers are still:

**gross, pre-fees, pre-slippage, pre-funding.**

So this is where we deliberately stop.

We are not adding another filter to “fix” the bad month.

We are not removing SOL.

We are not changing the TP or stop.

We are not searching for a better threshold.

The SHORT\_ONLY candidate is now frozen.

The next test will use an untouched Validation period:

**January 1, 2026 → May 1, 2026**

If the effect survives there, it becomes much more interesting.

If it fails, we record the failure instead of optimizing around it.

That is the whole point of the research process we’re building into BlackGreep:

**Discovery → Diagnose → Freeze → Validate**

No strategy edge has been established yet.

Would you move this candidate to Validation at this point, or would you require more Discovery evidence first?

comments.author: Appropriate-Talk-735
comments.body: It should do well in the new period since its a bearish one. I suggest you test the longs in a bullish regime. I would assume you have an edge if you run the longs only in bullish market and the shorts only in bearish market. PM me if you want to join my Discord with signals.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
That’s a fair hypothesis.

A regime-conditioned version — longs only in bullish regimes and shorts only in bearish regimes — is definitely worth testing.

The reason I’m not changing the current candidate now is that SHORT_ONLY has already been selected and frozen on Discovery data. Adding a regime filter before Validation would contaminate the test, especially if we already have an expectation about the next period being bearish.

So the current plan is:

1. Run the frozen SHORT_ONLY candidate on untouched Validation data.
2. Accept the result as-is, whether it works or fails.
3. Separately research a predeclared regime-adaptive version where direction depends on market regime.

That way we can distinguish whether SHORT_ONLY actually generalizes or whether we were just exploiting the regime in the Discovery sample.

And yes — the bullish LONG / bearish SHORT idea is one of the more interesting next hypotheses to test.

comments.author: OrganicFace5
comments.body:
I’d move it to Validation. Running more Discovery on the same 90 days would add no new evidence. But I’d go in with low expectations, and that is because of what I found in my own backtests and paper tradings.

I have run several hundred backtests across our engine catalog, ML classifiers, scoring layers and multi-timeframe stacks. At 1h and below we never found anything that held up, and 1m is lower still. Two things killed almost everything:

* **Costs.** A round trip is about 1 ATR at 5m on BTC, and worse at 1m.
* **Direction.** “Shorts work, longs don’t” usually turned out to be the market falling during the test window.

So before running Validation, I would:

1. Compute net R on Discovery, after fees, slippage and funding.
2. Run a random-direction control with the same exits.
3. Write down the pass/fail rule.

If net Discovery is already about zero, there is nothing left to validate.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
I think those are fair concerns, especially regarding costs and directional bias.

The SHORT_ONLY result could absolutely be a product of the market regime rather than a persistent edge. That's one of the main reasons I don't want to call the +49R result profitable or validated yet.

The Validation criteria were already defined before looking at that period, and the candidate is now frozen.

One thing I'm deliberately keeping separate is gross generalization versus execution survivability. The current plan is to run the unchanged strategy through untouched Validation first, then review Holdout, and finally evaluate how much of the observed expectancy survives fees, slippage and funding.

Your random-direction control is an interesting suggestion as well. I think it could be useful as a separate diagnostic, without using the result to retune the frozen candidate.

And I agree about the 1m cost problem. At +0.146R gross per trade, there's not exactly a huge cushion.

Have you found any particular execution or market conditions where short-timeframe strategies consistently survived realistic costs, or was the failure fairly universal across your tests?

replies.author: OrganicFace5
replies.body:
Fairly universal, but not uniform. Nothing at 1h or below survived realistic costs consistently across symbols, windows and bar alignments. A few conditions did move results in the same direction every time: limit entries instead of market entries (a filled limit and a limit take-profit pay no slippage), and stops wide enough that costs are a small share of them. Signal choice, scoring and multi-timeframe filters did not.

So my working conclusion is that at short timeframes, execution and cost structure decide more than the signal does. If I revisited 1m, I would start from maker-only entries and exits, a venue with fees you can actually get, and stops wide enough that costs stay a small share of them, and only then look at signals.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
That's a really useful distinction — execution structure improving results more consistently than signal complexity.

The fill assumption is what interests me most. Limit orders can reduce slippage, but only if we properly account for missed fills, partial fills and adverse selection. Otherwise it's easy to make a backtest look better by assuming favorable execution.

Our current 1m candidate uses next-open entries, so execution costs are definitely a major concern. I'm keeping that version frozen through Validation rather than changing the order model now.

But a separate maker-vs-taker execution study is something I'd like to explore afterward.

One question: when you tested limit entries, did you model queue position and missed fills, or use a simpler price-touch assumption?

I'm curious how much of the improvement survived once realistic fill probability was included.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Freezing the candidate before validation is the right move, and listing the bad month is what makes it credible. One thing I’d flag before validation: the long-short split was found by looking at the same 90 days, so “short-only” is itself a selection among options and counts toward the trial total. Fix the pass criteria in advance (minimum trades, net R after fees and slippage, per-market sign) so the Jan to May result can’t be read generously. Month 3 turning slightly negative also matters, so I’d check whether the edge decays over time in the validation period. If you want to see how a trading tool is built and tested in the open, the Build it Better page at Cymetica follows each app from request to verdict.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
That's an important distinction, and I agree.

SHORT_ONLY was selected after observing the Discovery results, so it absolutely counts as part of the research selection process. The +49R is not independent evidence of an edge.

We've already frozen the candidate and defined the gross Validation criteria, including sample size, cross-market consistency and concentration.

You're also right that gross Validation alone won't be enough. We plan to evaluate fees, slippage and funding separately, using fixed execution assumptions rather than adjusting them to rescue the results.

The negative third month is another reason we're tracking performance across four predefined monthly Validation blocks.

If the candidate fails, we'll record that result rather than optimize around it.

The broader goal with BlackGreep is to make selection bias, cost sensitivity and strategy failure visible instead of hiding them behind a profitable equity curve.

Appreciate the thoughtful feedback.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That covers the main points, and four predefined monthly blocks with fixed execution assumptions is a clean way to read it. Thanks for taking the feedback on board.
